```{r stats-helpers, include=FALSE}
# ---- Statistics boxes ------------------------------------------------------
# Every number in the "Statistics" boxes comes from output/paper/, written by
# the last section of code/02-05 (run with code/run_all.R). pn() stops the build if a number
# is missing, so a renamed key cannot silently drop a value.
paper_dir <- file.path("..", "..", "output", "paper")
paper_nums <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(
  list.files(paper_dir, pattern = "_numbers\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE),
  readr::read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE,
  col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character())
)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(estimate, ci_low, ci_high, statistic, df1, df2, p_value, n), as.numeric))
pn <- function(key) {
  d <- paper_nums[paper_nums$key == key, ]
  if (nrow(d) != 1) stop("pn(): no single number called ", key)
  d
}
fp   <- function(p) if (is.na(p)) "NA" else if (p < 0.001) "*p* < 0.001" else sprintf("*p* = %.3f", p)
fF   <- function(k) { d <- pn(k); sprintf("F~%s,%s~ = %.1f, %s", round(d$df1), round(d$df2), d$statistic, fp(d$p_value)) }
fchi <- function(k) { d <- pn(k); sprintf("χ²~%s~ = %.1f, %s", round(d$df1), d$statistic, fp(d$p_value)) }
fci  <- function(k, digits = 2) { d <- pn(k); sprintf("%.*f; 95%% CI %.*f–%.*f; %s", digits, d$estimate, digits, d$ci_low, digits, d$ci_high, fp(d$p_value)) }
est  <- function(k, digits = 2) sprintf("%.*f", digits, pn(k)$estimate)
frac <- function(k) { d <- pn(k); sprintf("%d of %d", as.integer(d$statistic), as.integer(d$n)) }
cnt  <- function(k, which = c("estimate", "statistic")) { d <- pn(k); sprintf("%d", as.integer(d[[match.arg(which)]])) }
nn   <- function(k) sprintf("%d", as.integer(pn(k)$n))
sens_tbl <- readr::read_csv(table_file("22b_sensitivity_wound_growth.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
sens_p <- function(resp, version) { d <- sens_tbl[sens_tbl$response == resp & sens_tbl$version == version, ]; stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1); fp(d$p_value) }
tank_txt <- function(lab) {
  d <- pn(paste0("budding_per_tank_", lab))
  if (d$estimate == d$statistic) sprintf("every %s tank, %d of %d", lab, as.integer(d$estimate), as.integer(d$n))
  else sprintf("%s tanks, between %d and %d of %d", lab, as.integer(d$estimate), as.integer(d$statistic), as.integer(d$n))
}
```

<div class="banner">
<strong>What we found:</strong> At 31 °C, coral fragments became paler, lost algae from their tissue, and gained less skeletal mass. Wounds still sealed, but only 4 of 12 heated fragments budded new corallites, the small skeletal cups on a regrown tip, by Day 15. All 12 fragments at 28 °C did so. Fragments from source patch C were less affected by heat than those from A and D.<br>
<strong>November 11 update:</strong> Every statistic was re-checked. Coral-condition tests now use the eight tanks as the temperature replicates. The heat effects held, with smaller but still clear test statistics. Two results softened: tip extension no longer clearly differs in timing between temperatures, and growth depends on one ambient tank. Each "Statistics" drop-down gives draft methods and results text, read directly from the analysis output.<br>
<strong>Genetic update:</strong> Final host-genotype groups are now available for the 144 early samples; the Day 15 fragments remain ungenotyped. A, C, and D still name the field source patches. Symbiont read typing remains rough.<br>
<strong>Species name:</strong> Species identification remains provisional: <em>Acropora cf. pulchra</em>. The abbreviation <em>cf.</em> means “compare with” and indicates that the species identification is uncertain. We retain <em>A. pulchra</em> here to match the project’s existing labels.
</div>

We kept coral fragments at <span class="t28">28 °C</span> or <span class="t31">31 °C</span> and clipped the growing tip on half of them. Over 15 days, we measured wound repair, skeletal growth, color, photosynthesis efficiency, and the algae living in coral tissue, called **algal symbionts**.

## The experiment

- 8 tanks: four held at <span class="t28">28 °C</span>, four at <span class="t31">31 °C</span>
- Half the fragments had the growing tip clipped; half were left unwounded
- 3 field source patches: A, C, D. A source patch is where the parent material came from; these patches are not yet confirmed genetic individuals.
- Tissue samples collected on Days 1, 3, 10, and 15
- The 48 fragments sampled on Day 15 were also followed for coral condition and regrowth; 24 were wounded
- A separate experiment followed wound covering in 16 wounded fragments using microscope photos

**Figure key.** The figures carry no legends; this key applies throughout. Temperature: <span class="t28">blue = 28 °C</span>, <span class="t31">orange = 31 °C</span>; where line type or symbol shape also marks temperature, 28 °C is solid with circles and 31 °C is dashed with triangles. Wounding: open symbols, white boxes and dashed lines mean unwounded; filled symbols, gray boxes and solid lines mean wounded (in the color-score figure, gray = unwounded and black = wounded; in the host-cluster symbiont figure, circles = unwounded and triangles = clipped). Source patches: gold = A, green = C, dark blue = D. Symbiont read groups: green = A, pink = B, gold = C, dark blue = D. An X marks a fragment that had not reached a stage by Day 15.

## What we found

### 1. The +3 °C temperature difference held

All eight tanks have 144 readings per day, one every ten minutes, from Day 0 through Day 15 (4–19 June 2025). Daily tank means averaged **27.78 °C** in the 28 °C treatment and **30.87 °C** in the 31 °C treatment, a **3.09 °C difference**. Each treatment had four tanks.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_apex}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("08_apex_temperature.png"))
```

The temperature record is complete through Day 15. Treatment averages exclude later days, after the main experiment ended.

**Water conditions during the experiment**

Handheld meter readings cover all eight tanks on 14 dates within 4–19 June: 112 tank-date observations. There are no meter readings for 4 or 7 June; these gaps do not affect the separate, continuous temperature record above.

```{r ysi-summary, echo=FALSE}
ysi_overall <- read.csv(here::here("output/tables/09_ysi_study_summary.csv"))
ysi_treatment <- read.csv(here::here("output/tables/09_ysi_treatment_summary.csv"))
ysi_vars <- c("sal", "do_mgl", "ph")
ysi_fmt <- function(d) {
  d <- d[match(ysi_vars, d$variable), ]
  sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", d$mean, d$sd_readings)
}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Measure=c("Salinity (unitless)", "Dissolved oxygen (mg/L)", "pH"),
  `All tanks`=ysi_fmt(ysi_overall),
  `28 °C`=ysi_fmt(subset(ysi_treatment, treatment == "28C")),
  `31 °C`=ysi_fmt(subset(ysi_treatment, treatment == "31C")),
  check.names=FALSE), row.names=FALSE)
```

Values are means ± standard deviations, which describe variation across tanks and sampled dates. Each temperature includes four tanks and 56 readings. Repeated readings are not additional independent tanks. The sheet identifies dissolved oxygen as **milligrams per liter (mg/L)** and salinity as unitless; it does not specify the pH scale.

Salinity and pH varied little in these spot checks. Dissolved oxygen concentration was lower in the heated tanks, so these measurements do not establish that temperature was the only water condition that differed. Spot checks also cannot rule out changes between visits.

```{r, fig.cap="Water conditions measured with a handheld YSI meter during 4–19 June 2025. Each line follows one tank; points are recorded readings, with four tanks per temperature. Panels have different vertical scales. Temperature is converted from the sheet’s Fahrenheit readings to Celsius; dissolved oxygen is in mg/L, and salinity and pH are unitless. All tanks were measured on 14 dates. No readings are available for 4 or 7 June; connecting lines do not represent measurements or filled values on missing dates."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("09_ysi_water_chem.png"))
```

<details class="stats">
<summary>Statistics: methods and results for tank temperature and water quality</summary>

##### What was measured
Water temperature in all eight tanks every 10 minutes, Day 0 (June 4, the day tips were clipped) to Day 15 (June 19). Salinity, dissolved oxygen and pH with a handheld meter, once per tank on `r round(pn("ysi_sal")$df1)` of those 16 days (none on June 4 or 7), for `r nn("ysi_sal")` readings.

##### Methods text (draft)
<div class="ms">An Apex controller (Neptune Systems) recorded water temperature in each tank every 10 min. We averaged the readings for each tank on each day, then averaged those daily values across the four tanks in each treatment for Days 0–15. Salinity, dissolved oxygen and pH were measured with a handheld YSI meter (ProQuatro) in all eight tanks on `r round(pn("ysi_sal")$df1)` days between June 4 and 19, 2025; no readings were taken on June 4 or 7.</div>

##### Results text (draft)
<div class="ms">Tanks averaged `r est("temp_mean_ambient")` °C in the ambient treatment and `r est("temp_mean_heated")` °C in the heated treatment, a difference of `r est("temp_difference")` °C. Daily tank averages stayed between `r sprintf("%.2f", pn("temp_mean_ambient")$ci_low)` and `r sprintf("%.2f", pn("temp_mean_ambient")$ci_high)` °C in ambient tanks and between `r sprintf("%.2f", pn("temp_mean_heated")$ci_low)` and `r sprintf("%.2f", pn("temp_mean_heated")$ci_high)` °C in heated tanks. Across all `r nn("ysi_sal")` meter readings (mean ± SD), salinity was `r sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", pn("ysi_sal")$estimate, pn("ysi_sal")$statistic)`, dissolved oxygen `r sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", pn("ysi_do_mgl")$estimate, pn("ysi_do_mgl")$statistic)` mg/L, and pH `r sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", pn("ysi_ph")$estimate, pn("ysi_ph")$statistic)`. Dissolved oxygen was lower in heated tanks (`r sprintf("%.2f", pn("ysi_do_heated")$estimate)` vs `r sprintf("%.2f", pn("ysi_do_ambient")$estimate)` mg/L).</div>

##### Where the numbers come from
<p class="src">`output/paper/tanks_water_numbers.csv`, written by `code/02_tanks_water.R`.</p>

<div class="dont">

**Open question:** the pH scale (NBS or total) is not recorded in the YSI sheet. Molly has been asked.

</div>

</details>

### 2. Heat reduced coral condition; average growth was also lower

At <span class="t31">31 °C</span>, fragments became paler, gained less skeletal mass, and lost algal symbionts. Their photosynthesis-efficiency score, **Fv/Fm**, also fell. This score measures how efficiently the algae’s photosynthetic system can use light.

These changes occurred in clipped and unwounded fragments. We found little evidence that tip clipping added to the decline caused by heat. This does not establish that clipping has no effect, or that a local wound response is absent. For symbionts, the clipping result depends on which tanks are included. Where there was a difference, heated clipped fragments kept *more* symbionts than heated unwounded ones.

- Photosynthesis score and color declined through time under heat.
- Symbiont density dropped sharply over the two weeks.
- Skeletal mass gain was **34% lower** at <span class="t31">31 °C</span>. Because temperature was assigned to tanks, the test uses four tanks per treatment as the independent replicates (`r fp(pn("growth_temp")$p_value)`). A stricter tank permutation check gives `r fp(pn("growth_tank_permutation")$p_value)`, so treat this as moderate evidence. It leans on ambient tank 3, which grew about as little as the heated tanks: without tank 3 the test gives `r sens_p("growth", "without ambient tank 3")`, and leaving out tank 12 instead gives `r sens_p("growth", "leave one tank out: highest p")`.

**Heat and wounding across three measures of coral condition**

Source patches are combined in this display, not removed from the models. Day 0 marks clipping; Day −1 is not an unheated baseline. Missing values are not filled."}

<details class="stats">
<summary>Statistics: methods and results for photosynthesis, color, symbionts and growth</summary>

##### What was measured
- **Photosynthetic efficiency (Fv/Fm):** how well the algae in the coral tissue use light, measured with a PAM fluorometer on dark-adapted fragments. Two readings per fragment (near the tip and near the base), averaged. Same 48 fragments on Days −1, 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 and 14.
- **Color:** CoralWatch color-card score from 1 (palest) to 6 (darkest), same 48 fragments, Days −4 to 14.
- **Symbiont density:** algal cells per cm² of coral surface. Each fragment could be sampled only once, so each sampling day (1, 3, 10, 15) used different fragments: 12 per temperature × wound combination per day, 192 in total.
- **Growth:** percentage change in buoyant (skeletal) mass from Day 0 to Day 15, same 48 fragments.

Temperature was set at the tank level, with four tanks per temperature. Each tank held fragments from all three source patches, wounded and unwounded.

##### Methods text (draft)
<div class="ms">We analysed Fv/Fm and color score with linear mixed models. Fixed effects were temperature, wound status, day and source patch, with all their interactions, and day entered as a linear trend. Because temperature was applied to whole tanks and fragments were measured repeatedly, each model included a random intercept and a random day slope for each tank, and a random intercept for each fragment. The tank slopes make the temperature × day test use tanks as the replicates. Symbiont density was log-transformed because it varied several-fold among fragments. It was analysed with the same fixed effects and a random intercept and day slope for each tank; each fragment was sampled once. Growth was analysed with temperature, wound status, source patch and their interactions, and a random intercept for tank. We fitted models with lme4 and lmerTest in R and used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Because temperature was applied to whole tanks, the temperature test for growth uses tanks as the replicates (4 per temperature). As a check, we also compared the four ambient and four heated tank means against all 70 possible ways of assigning four tanks to each treatment (an exact permutation test; reported in the supplement).</div>

##### Results text (draft)
<div class="ms">Fv/Fm declined over time in heated fragments but not in ambient fragments (temperature × day, `r fF("pam_temp_x_day")`). By Day 14, heated fragments averaged `r est("pam_day14_heated")` and ambient fragments `r est("pam_day14_ambient")`. Wounded and unwounded fragments declined at similar rates (temperature × wound × day, `r fF("pam_temp_x_wound_x_day")`).

Heated fragments also became paler over time (temperature × day, `r fF("color_temp_x_day")`), ending at a mean color score of `r est("color_final_heated", 1)` compared with `r est("color_final_ambient", 1)` at ambient. The change in color again did not differ between wounded and unwounded fragments (temperature × wound × day, `r fF("color_temp_x_wound_x_day")`).

Symbiont density fell over time under heat (temperature × day, `r fF("zoox_temp_x_day")`). By Day 15, heated fragments held `r est("zoox_day15_heated")` million cells per cm², compared with `r est("zoox_day15_ambient")` million at ambient. Wounding did not clearly change this pattern (temperature × wound × day, `r fF("zoox_temp_x_wound_x_day")`), but this term depends on individual tanks and fragments: leaving out one tank gives *p* values from `r sub("\\*p\\* = ", "", sens_p("symbionts", "leave one tank out: lowest p"))` to `r sub("\\*p\\* = ", "", sens_p("symbionts", "leave one tank out: highest p"))`. Where there was a difference, heated wounded fragments kept more symbionts than heated unwounded ones, not fewer.

Heated fragments gained `r est("growth_pct_lower", 0)`% less skeletal mass over 15 days than ambient fragments (`r est("growth_heated")`% vs `r est("growth_ambient")`%; temperature, `r fF("growth_temp")`). Wounded and unwounded fragments grew similarly (wound, `r fF("growth_wound")`; temperature × wound, `r fF("growth_temp_x_wound")`).</div>

##### Where the numbers come from
<p class="src">`output/paper/physiology_numbers.csv`, written by `code/03_physiology.R` (models in section 1, Figure 2 means in section 5, the tank permutation in section 4).</p>

<div class="dont">

**Growth test (decided Nov 10):** report the model test in the text. The tank permutation (`r fp(pn("growth_tank_permutation")$p_value)`) goes in the supplement as a check; it agrees in direction but sits just above 0.05, so describe the growth effect as moderate evidence rather than a strong result.

**Out of date (Nov 11):** *F* values for temperature × day from before Nov 11 (for example Fv/Fm *F* = 120 on 228 df) came from models without tank day slopes, which treated every measurement as independent evidence about the slope. They overstated the evidence; use the numbers above (about 6–7 denominator df).

**Out of date:** earlier drafts gave wound *p* = 0.351 and temperature × wound *p* = 0.908 for growth. Those predate the correction of fragment 119 to wounded.

**Wording:** "no difference between wounded and unwounded" means we found no evidence of one with 12 fragments per group. It does not show that wounding has no effect.

</div>

</details>

### 3. Wounds re-covered, but fewer heated fragments budded new corallites

Wounds re-covered with living tissue quickly at both temperatures. Only **4 of 12 heated fragments (33%)** had budded new corallites, the small skeletal cups on the rebuilt tip, by Day 15. All **12 of 12 fragments at 28 °C (100%)** had done so. A longer experiment might have allowed more heated fragments to reach this step; these data cannot tell us whether the delay was permanent.

Here, **healing** means the coenosarc, the sheet of living tissue between coral polyps, re-covered the wound. **Regeneration** means the later rebuilding steps: the main polyp forms, the wound surface remodels, the tip returns, the tip extends, and new corallites bud.

The healing panel uses a separate microscope-photo experiment with 16 wounded fragments, eight per temperature. The other panels use the 24 wounded fragments in the main experiment, 12 per temperature. All 16 microscope fragments were recorded as covered on Day 1. The microscope photos illustrate the stages in a separate group; they cannot verify individual scores in the main experiment.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_stage_cumulative}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("39d_stage_cumulative_all_stages.png"))
```

The manuscript's Figure 1B (`39b_stage_timing_cumulative_option`) shows four of these panels, the regeneration milestones 1, 3, 4 and 5, all from the main experiment.

The gap opened before Day 15. By Day 8, `r frac("tip_extension_pct_day8_ambient")` ambient fragments had an extending tip, compared with `r frac("tip_extension_pct_day8_heated")` heated fragments. By Day 12, `r frac("budding_pct_day12_ambient")` ambient fragments had budded new corallites, compared with `r frac("budding_pct_day12_heated")` heated fragments.

The curves show the percentage first recorded at each stage by each day. Each percentage includes all fragments, including those that had not reached the stage. Once a fragment has a positive score, it remains counted, even if a later score marks the feature absent. A later absence may reflect a real change or a scoring inconsistency; these curves do not distinguish the two.

```{r}
stage_summary_tbl <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path("..", "..", "output", "tables", "36_stage_timing_mean_iqr.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
stage_names <- c("Living tissue covers wound", "Main polyp forms",
                 "Wound surface remodels", "Tip forms", "Tip extends",
                 "New skeletal cups bud")
attainment <- stage_summary_tbl |>
  dplyr::mutate(Stage = stage_names[stage_order],
                value = sprintf("%d/%d (%.0f%%)", n_reached, n_scored, pct_reached)) |>
  dplyr::select(Stage, treatment, value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = treatment, values_from = value)
knitr::kable(attainment, caption = paste(
  "Fragments observed at each stage at least once by Day 15.",
  "Tissue cover uses the separate microscope-photo experiment; other rows use the main experiment."
))
```

This differs from asking whether a feature was **present on Day 15 itself**. The table and curves show whether each fragment had reached a stage at least once by that day. They do not assume that every stage follows a fixed order or that a feature remains visible afterward.

**Average time to each stage.** Average first-observation days are shown only for stages that every fragment reached at both temperatures. For stages some fragments never reached, an average describes only the fragments that finished, so it is not shown.


```{r}
complete_timing <- stage_summary_tbl |>
  dplyr::filter(complete_both_temperatures) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Stage = stage_names[stage_order], Temperature = treatment,
                   `Mean first-observation day` = mean_day,
                   `Middle half of first days` = iqr_days)
knitr::kable(complete_timing, digits = 2, caption = paste(
  "Timing summaries for stages reached by all fragments at both temperatures.",
  "The middle-half range runs from the 25th to the 75th percentile.",
  "These are first observation days, not exact biological onset times.",
  "All 16 microscope fragments had tissue cover recorded on Day 1."
))
```

**Individual timing and unfinished stages.** The distributions below show when fragments reached each stage, with unfinished stages retained above the day axis.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_molly_stage_violin}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("36b_stage_violin.png"))
```

<details>
<summary>Exact observation days for each fragment</summary>

```{r, fig.cap=cap_molly_stage_timing}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("36_stage_timing.png"))
```

</details>


**What the scores tell us.** The reviewed records show tip formation in 11 of 12 fragments at each temperature, rather than all 12. Budding can occur in the wound area before visible tip extension, so these stages are not a strict sequence. The budding result remains 12/12 at 28 °C versus 4/12 at 31 °C.

Pigment was assessed on Days 3, 4, 9, 12, and 15 in the main experiment. Other days remain unknown, not absent. Pigment is not one of the six stages above, and its sparse observations support a less precise timing comparison.

<details>
<summary>Other daily observations (polyps, pigment, algae, flatworms)</summary>

```{r, fig.cap=cap_other_obs}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("47_other_daily_observations.png"))
```

</details>

**How the timing models handle unfinished stages.** A fragment that had not reached a stage by its final observation contributes “not yet reached” information. It is not dropped or assigned an invented completion day. For fragments that did reach a stage, the main timing model places onset between the last absent score and the first present score.

The timing model estimates a **`r est("new_corallites_on_tip_time_ratio")`-fold longer time** to new-corallite budding at 31 °C. This is a model estimate, not the average time of the four heated fragments that budded. It assumes a particular pattern of event times (a log-logistic distribution, chosen because it fitted these data best) and adjusts for source patch. Its uncertainty does not account for fragments sharing a tank. The observed 4/12 versus 12/12 result does not depend on that model, and it held in every tank: every ambient tank had 3 of 3 wounded fragments bud and every heated tank 1 of 3. The same models found no clear temperature difference in when the tip extended.

A closed wound is not the same thing as a regenerated tip. If we scored only wound sealing, we would miss the main heat effect.

The two fragments shown below both seal the wound and rebuild a tip. Only the fragment at 28 °C buds new corallites by Day 15.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_timeline}
knitr::include_graphics(img("slide15_morphology_timeline.jpg"))
```

The time-lapse follows these two fragments from Day 0 to Day 15: 28 °C on the left and 31 °C on the right.

<details class="stats">
<summary>Statistics: methods and results for healing and regeneration</summary>

##### What was measured
**Main experiment:** the 24 wounded fragments among the 48 followed to Day 15 (12 per temperature) were scored every day from Day 0 to Day 15. Each day we recorded whether each of five regeneration stages was present:

1. The main (axial) polyp forms in the cut surface.
2. The cut surface smooths over.
3. A new tip forms.
4. The tip extends.
5. New radial corallites (the small skeletal cups) bud on the tip.

**Separate microscope experiment:** 16 other wounded fragments (8 per temperature), photographed daily under a dissecting microscope. Only this experiment recorded when living tissue first covered the cut. It used different tanks and only two source patches, so it is analysed separately.

##### Methods text (draft)
<div class="ms">For each fragment and stage, we recorded the first day the stage was seen. We compared the number of fragments that reached each stage by Day 15 between temperatures with Fisher's exact tests. To compare how long fragments took to reach a stage, we used time-to-event models. Because fragments were scored once a day, each stage began at some point between the last check without it and the first check with it. Interval-censored log-logistic models use that interval rather than assuming the stage began exactly on the day it was first seen. We chose the log-logistic distribution because it fitted best, or within 0.6 AIC of the best, for every stage among Weibull, lognormal, log-logistic and exponential. Fragments that had not reached a stage by Day 15 were kept in the analysis as "not yet reached", not dropped. Models included source patch, and we checked the results with Cox proportional-hazards models and log-rank tests on the first day each stage was seen (survival package in R). Because temperature was applied to whole tanks, we also report the outcome for each tank and an exact permutation test of the four ambient and four heated tanks.</div>

##### Results text (draft)
<div class="ms">In the microscope experiment, living tissue covered the cut by Day 1 in all `r cnt("tissue_cover_by_day1")` of `r nn("tissue_cover_by_day1")` fragments at both temperatures. In the main experiment, nearly every fragment at both temperatures formed an axial polyp (`r cnt("axial_polyp_formation_reached_by_day15")`/`r nn("axial_polyp_formation_reached_by_day15")` ambient, `r cnt("axial_polyp_formation_reached_by_day15", "statistic")`/`r nn("axial_polyp_formation_reached_by_day15")` heated), smoothed the cut surface (`r cnt("wound_smoothed_reached_by_day15")`/12, `r cnt("wound_smoothed_reached_by_day15", "statistic")`/12) and formed a new tip (`r cnt("tip_exist_reached_by_day15")`/12, `r cnt("tip_exist_reached_by_day15", "statistic")`/12). Heat mainly affected the last stage. By Day 15, `r cnt("new_corallites_on_tip_reached_by_day15")` of 12 ambient fragments had budded new radial corallites, compared with `r cnt("new_corallites_on_tip_reached_by_day15", "statistic")` of 12 heated fragments (Fisher's exact test, `r fp(pn("new_corallites_on_tip_present_day15")$p_value)`). The pattern held tank by tank: in `r tank_txt("ambient")` wounded fragments budded; in `r tank_txt("heated")` did (exact tank permutation, `r fp(pn("budding_tank_permutation")$p_value)`, the smallest value possible with four tanks per temperature). A time-to-event model estimated that budding took about `r est("new_corallites_on_tip_time_ratio", 1)` times as long under heat (time ratio `r fci("new_corallites_on_tip_time_ratio")`). On any given day, heated fragments were about one-fifth as likely to bud as ambient fragments (Cox hazard ratio `r fci("budding_hazard_ratio")`). Tip extension was reached by `r cnt("tip_extension_reached_by_day15")` of 12 ambient and `r cnt("tip_extension_reached_by_day15", "statistic")` of 12 heated fragments and its timing did not differ clearly between temperatures (time ratio `r fci("tip_extension_time_ratio")`).</div>

##### Where the numbers come from
<p class="src">`output/paper/regeneration_numbers.csv`, written by `code/04_regeneration.R` (stage counts and Fisher tests in section 1, timing models in section 2, reached-by-Day-15 counts in section 3, tank counts and tissue cover in section 5).</p>

<div class="dont">

**To confirm:** whether the daily scores were made by eye or from the color-card photos (asked of Molly, Nov 10). Color-card photos exist for only 7 of the 16 days.

**Counts differ by definition:** the Fisher counts use whether a stage was present on the last scored day, so tip extension there is `r cnt("tip_extension_present_day15")` vs `r cnt("tip_extension_present_day15", "statistic")`. The "reached by Day 15" counts above give `r cnt("tip_extension_reached_by_day15")` vs `r cnt("tip_extension_reached_by_day15", "statistic")`.

**Tanks:** the timing models, the Cox model and the Fisher and log-rank tests treat each fragment as independent, but three wounded fragments shared each tank. Use the time ratio and hazard ratio as effect sizes; for significance, cite the per-tank counts and the tank permutation.

**Out of date (Nov 11):** earlier drafts used Weibull timing models, which fitted these intervals worst and gave tip extension a time ratio of 1.36 (*p* = 0.023, "took somewhat longer under heat"). The log-logistic models do not show a clear difference for tip extension. Budding is unchanged in direction and size.

**Don't report:**

- *p*-values from the daily yes/no models (frozen in `extras/`: `12_morph_*`, `12c_*`, and the "Morphology" rows of `20_master_results.csv`), including the planned tip-extension test. Their results change with the computer and package versions (2026-11-10 rerun check; see `code/README.md`).
- the average day each stage was reached, for stages some fragments never reached. For budding under heat, that average describes only 4 of 12 fragments.

**Source patches:** every ambient fragment budded, but under heat budding differed by source patch: `r cnt("budding_heated_patch_A")` of `r nn("budding_heated_patch_A")` from patch A, `r cnt("budding_heated_patch_C")` of `r nn("budding_heated_patch_C")` from C and `r cnt("budding_heated_patch_D")` of `r nn("budding_heated_patch_D")` from D. With four fragments per group, and no budding at all in heated patch A, the Cox source patch × temperature test cannot be estimated reliably, so report these counts rather than its *p*-value. Treat this as a pattern to follow up, not a result.

</div>

</details>

### 4. Source patch C was hurt less by heat

Fragments from **source patch C** retained more of their photosynthesis efficiency, color, and algal symbionts under heat than fragments from A and D. Growth followed the same pattern, but the evidence for a growth difference is weaker.

We compare each patch at 31 °C with the same patch at 28 °C. That tells us how much heat changed its response, rather than which patch had the highest starting value.

The condition measurements consistently point to smaller heat effects in C. The size of the difference depends on the response and its measurement scale; there is no single fold difference that describes C's heat tolerance.

```{r, fig.cap="Heat lowered every measurement less in source patch C. Each panel shows the mean for fragments from patches A, C and D at the end of the experiment: Fv/Fm and color on Day 14, symbiont density on Day 15 (log scale), and growth over Days 0–15. Bars show one standard error across fragments (8 per patch and temperature), not tank-level uncertainty. Lines that are not parallel mean the heat effect differs among patches. These are raw means; the formal tests are in the Statistics drop-down below."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("13_genet_response_panel.png"))
```

<details class="stats">
<summary>Statistics: methods and results for source-patch differences</summary>

##### What was measured
The same physiology measurements as above, split by source patch. A source patch is the field patch (A, C or D) a fragment's parent branch came from. Each patch contributed 16 fragments to the 48 followed to Day 15, split evenly across temperatures and wound status.

##### Methods text (draft)
<div class="ms">To test whether the effect of heat differed among source patches, we refitted each physiology model without all terms involving source patch × temperature (including their interactions with wound status and day). We compared the full and reduced models with likelihood-ratio tests. We then estimated the ambient-minus-heated difference for each patch at Day 14 from the full model.</div>

##### Results text (draft)
<div class="ms">The effect of heat differed among source patches for Fv/Fm (`r fchi("patch_x_temp_pam_fvfm")`), color (`r fchi("patch_x_temp_color_dscale")`) and symbiont density (`r fchi("patch_x_temp_log_zoox")`). The evidence for growth was weaker (`r fchi("patch_x_temp_growth_pct")`). Fragments from patch C were affected least. By Day 14, heat lowered Fv/Fm by `r est("heat_drop_pam_fvfm_patch_C", 3)` in patch C, compared with `r est("heat_drop_pam_fvfm_patch_A", 3)` in A and `r est("heat_drop_pam_fvfm_patch_D", 3)` in D (model estimates averaged over wound status). Color fell by `r est("heat_drop_color_dscale_patch_C", 1)` points in C, compared with `r est("heat_drop_color_dscale_patch_A", 1)` in A and `r est("heat_drop_color_dscale_patch_D", 1)` in D.</div>

##### Where the numbers come from
<p class="src">`output/paper/source_patches_numbers.csv`, written by `code/05_source_patches.R`, using per-patch heat effects from the `code/03_physiology.R` models.</p>

<div class="dont">

**Source patches vs genotypes:** source patches are field labels, not confirmed genotypes. Rachael's final SNP clusters place all 48 sequenced patch C fragments in one cluster, while A and D each contain several.

**Out of date (Nov 11):** earlier versions of this test compared 14 df (6 for growth) because they also dropped patch × wound and patch × day terms. The test now drops only the terms that contain source patch × temperature, as the methods text says (8 df; 4 for growth).

**Per-patch heat effects:** six contrasts per response (three patches × wound status). Holm-adjusted *p* values are in `output/tables/12_genet_treatment_effects.csv` (`p_holm`). The patch C estimates are the smallest and least certain.

**What this can show:** with three patches, this describes differences among these patches. It does not estimate how much heat tolerance varies among genotypes in the population.

</div>

</details>

### 5. Final DNA-marker groups and the algae they host

The final DNA-marker results group fragments by genetic similarity. The markers are **single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)**, differences at individual DNA positions. They came from **RNA sequencing (RNA-seq)**, which measures gene activity and can also reveal some DNA differences.

A group of genetically similar samples is called a **cluster**. The final set has eight host-genotype clusters. All 144 fragments retain their earlier cluster assignments; the final genetic-coordinate values replace the preliminary values. These assignments apply to the sequenced fragments, not automatically to other fragments collected from the same source patch.

The file matches 144 tissue samples prepared for sequencing, called **libraries**, using each fragment’s identifying number:

- All **48 samples from C** fall in cluster 1.
- The 48 samples from A fall in clusters 4, 5, 6, and 7, mostly cluster 4.
- The 48 samples from D fall in clusters 2, 3, 4, 5, and 8.
- A and D share clusters 4 and 5.

```{r, fig.cap="Final host-genotype clusters preserve the earlier group memberships. Left: each point is one of 144 sequenced fragments, positioned using the first two summaries of DNA-marker differences from the final SNP set. Colors identify field source patches. Right: counts in each genetic cluster, split by source patch; labels identify the larger segments. Cluster sizes are 48, 17, 16, 52, 7, 2, 1, and 1. Host clusters and source patches are different groupings."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_structure.png"))
```

All sequenced fragments from source patch C belong to host cluster 1. A and D each contain several clusters and share clusters 4 and 5. We assigned treatments by source patch before these genetic results were available. Final assignments do not fix the resulting imbalance: some clusters have few samples or no samples in particular treatment combinations.

```{r, fig.cap="Final clusters are unevenly represented across treatments. Each tile gives the number of sequenced fragments for a host cluster, temperature, sampling day, and clipping treatment. Zero means an empty combination, not a missing genetic assignment. Clusters 7 and 8 have only heated samples; cluster 6 has one fragment per temperature. These groups cannot support a well-replicated comparison of heat responses."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_design.png"))
```

**Which responses can we link to DNA markers?** The current 144 sequenced fragments were sampled on Days 1, 3, and 10. Symbiont density is the only response measured on those same fragments that we can directly link to these markers.

The 48 fragments sampled on Day 15 have the broader response record: photosynthesis score and color through Day 14, growth and symbiont density at Day 15, and regrowth through Day 15. We do not yet have DNA-marker results for those fragments.

The current plan is to move ahead with the existing samples rather than delay the paper for new sequencing. The final host assignments can inform expression analyses where treatment combinations overlap. They do not add Day 15 genetic assignments or gene-expression measurements.

```{r, fig.cap="Measured symbiont density within final host clusters. Each point is one fragment; color distinguishes temperature and shape distinguishes clipping. Sampling days remain separate rather than being pooled into a genetic effect. The vertical scale shows millions of algal cells per square centimeter, with equal spacing for equal fold changes. Small horizontal offsets separate overlapping points. These are observations, not adjusted treatment estimates, and fragments in a tank are not independent temperature replicates."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_symbiont_density.png"))
```

The updated density analysis accounts for tank, sampling day, clipping, and host cluster. It retains a smaller estimated heat-related loss in cluster 1 than in clusters 2–4. This pattern remains when we leave out fragments dominated by other symbiont groups. It is a reanalysis of the same density data, not independent confirmation of genetic control. Small, uneven groups and imperfect model fit keep these comparisons exploratory; clusters 6–8 are shown but not included in the fitted cluster comparisons.

**Which algae dominate?** The new file also compares sequence reads with four reference symbiont genomes. A read is a short piece of sequence; the relative share mapping to each reference provides a rough picture of the symbiont mixture. Group A, identified as *Symbiodinium*, dominates **138 of 144 fragments**. Five are dominated by group D and one by C. These symbiont letters are unrelated to our coral source-patch letters or host-cluster numbers.

```{r, fig.cap="Rough symbiont typing from sequence-read mapping. Each bar is a fragment; colored portions show the reported relative shares for reference groups A, B, C, and D, which sum to one. Panels are final host clusters, with sample counts shown; bar widths therefore differ among panels. Fragments are ordered by their group-A share, not by time. These shares are not measured cell proportions or symbiont density, and a dominant group does not imply that no other group is present."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_symbiont_typing.png"))
```

All six non-A-dominated fragments were heated and clipped; five were sampled on Day 10 and one on Day 1. We cannot tell from these data whether heat changed their symbiont mixture or whether they differed beforehand. This makes the mixture worth checking in expression analyses, but it is not evidence that symbiont type caused the heat response. Host assignments are final; this symbiont typing remains rough, and updated expression results are still pending.

## Take-homes

- **The +3 °C difference held.** All eight tanks have a complete temperature record through Day 15 (mean difference 3.09 °C). Dissolved oxygen was lower in the heated tanks, so temperature was not the only water condition that differed.
- **Heat reduced coral condition.** Over two weeks at 31 °C, Fv/Fm, color and symbiont density all declined, and these effects are clear with the eight tanks as the replicates. Growth was 34% lower, but that result is weaker: it depends on one ambient tank that grew little.
- **Clipping added little to the heat effect.** Clipped and unwounded fragments declined at similar rates. For symbionts the result depends on which tanks are included, and where there was a difference, clipped heated fragments kept *more* symbionts, not fewer.
- **Heat stalled the last step of regrowth, not wound repair.** Wounds re-covered within a day at both temperatures, and nearly every fragment formed a main polyp, smoothed the cut and grew a new tip. Budding of new corallites differed: 12 of 12 ambient versus 4 of 12 heated fragments by Day 15, and the pattern held in every tank. We cannot tell whether the heated fragments would have budded later.
- **Source patch C was least affected.** Heat lowered Fv/Fm, color and symbiont density less in C than in A or D, and the formal patch × temperature tests agree. All 48 sequenced fragments from C belong to one host cluster, so patch and genotype can't be separated for C.
- **Genetic and symbiont data are limited by the design.** Final host clusters are available only for the 144 fragments sampled on Days 1, 3 and 10, and are unevenly spread across treatments. Most fragments host mainly group-A symbionts; the six exceptions were all heated and clipped.

## Open questions

What the current data can and cannot say about each question, as of November 12, 2026.

- **Was budding delayed or blocked?** Partly answered, not resolved. At 28 °C, the `r nn("bud_lag_ambient")` fragments with both events recorded budded `r est("bud_lag_ambient", 0)` to `r cnt("bud_lag_ambient", "statistic")` days after their tip began to extend; the twelfth budded on Day 15 with no tip extension recorded. At 31 °C, `r cnt("bud_stalled_heated")` of 12 fragments had an extending tip for longer than that and still had not budded by Day 15. The last heated fragment to bud did so on Day `r cnt("budding_first_day_range_heated", "statistic")`. The separate microscope experiment showed the same pattern: `r cnt("micro_budding_day15_heated")` of 8 heated fragments had budded by Day 15, compared with `r cnt("micro_budding_day15_ambient")` of 8 at 28 °C. So heat slowed or stalled the step from tip extension to budding. These data cannot separate a long delay from a permanent block: whether those fragments would bud given more time, or after a return to 28 °C, needs a longer experiment.
- **What makes patch C more tolerant?** Partly answered: patch C carried a second symbiont group alongside the usual one. In the 28 °C samples, `r cnt("sym_D_over5pct_28C_patch_C")` of 24 patch C samples had more than 5% of their symbiont reads in group D, compared with `r cnt("sym_D_over5pct_28C_patch_A")` of 24 from patch A and `r cnt("sym_D_over5pct_28C_patch_D")` of 24 from patch D. Patch C also budded more often under heat: `r cnt("budding_heated_patch_C")` of the 4 heated fragments that budded came from C. The genus of group D is not confirmed: the letters are Rachael's reference labels, and she has confirmed only that group A is *Symbiodinium*. If group D turned out to be *Durusdinium*, a genus often linked to heat tolerance, that would fit the pattern, but this is a question for Rachael, not a finding. The read shares are rough, and patch C is a single host cluster from one field patch. Host genotype, symbionts and field history therefore still travel together. Separating them would need patch C hosts with and without the group D symbionts, or more genotypes per patch.
- **Which gene responses go with slower regrowth?** Not answerable yet. The expression counts have not been delivered; Rachael and Shreya are rerunning the processing. Two limits apply when they arrive. The expression samples come from Days 1, 3 and 10, before any fragment budded. They are also destructively sampled fragments, not the fragments scored for budding. Expression can therefore test group differences (heat, clipping, and whether patch C responds differently), but it cannot link one fragment's genes to that fragment's regrowth.
- **Did lower oxygen in the heated tanks contribute?** Probably not much, but these data cannot rule it out. Heated tanks averaged `r est("ysi_do_heated")` mg/L of oxygen, compared with `r est("ysi_do_ambient")` mg/L in ambient tanks. Warmer water holds less oxygen, which alone accounts for `r est("do_solubility_drop")` mg/L of the `r sprintf("%.2f", pn("do_solubility_drop")$statistic)` mg/L difference. Tanks stayed above saturation on average (heated `r est("ysi_do_pct_heated", 0)`%, ambient `r est("ysi_do_pct_ambient", 0)`%), and the lowest single reading was `r sprintf("%.0f", pn("ysi_do_pct_heated")$ci_low)`%. We have not tested whether oxygen tracked coral condition across tanks; with four tanks per temperature such a test would have little power. Readings were taken between late morning and evening, so night-time oxygen, when it is lowest, is unknown, and daytime spot checks cannot exclude night-time effects.
- **Does clipping change symbiont loss under heat?** The direction is consistent, but its size is not settled. Under heat, clipped fragments kept somewhat more symbionts late in the experiment: `r est("zoox_heated_wound_ratio_day10")` times the unclipped mean on Day 10 and `r est("zoox_heated_wound_ratio_day15")` times on Day 15. Clipped fragments had more on both days in `r cnt("zoox_heated_tanks_wounded_higher")` of 4 heated tanks. Clipping did not speed symbiont loss; if anything, it slowed it. The model test (`r fF("zoox_temp_x_wound_x_day")`) shifts with which tank is left out, and each tank contributes only three fragments per group and day. A run with more tanks per temperature would settle it.

## How much confidence to place in the results

The observed wound-cover and budding counts do not depend on a fitted timing model. Temperature was assigned to tanks, so the four tanks per treatment, not the individual fragments, are the independent temperature replicates. Since November 11 the coral-condition models allow each tank its own trend over time, so their temperature tests rest on the tanks. Heat effects remained clear, and they held without the flagged fragments and tank. Growth and budding also have tank-by-tank permutation tests. Each model and test was checked for fit, influence and alternative structures; the audit is in `docs/diagnostics/MODEL_DIAGNOSTICS_2026-11-11.md`.

Some daily yes/no morphology models have unstable estimates because nearly every fragment shares the same score at some stages. We do not use their very small reported *p*-values as evidence. Repair-timing *p*-values treat fragments as independent, and the tip-extension timing result depended on the chosen distribution, so we do not report a timing difference there. With only three source patches, patch differences describe these patches, not variation across the population. The genetic-cluster comparisons are uneven and remain exploratory.
